analysis.one_liner: Designates millions of acres of Northern Rockies public land as wilderness, off-limits to logging, mining, and new roads.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 64 cosponsors and held subcommittee hearings, but never reached a House floor vote before Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set aside large wild areas in Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming as wilderness, wild and scenic rivers, and biological corridors connecting them, protecting habitat for grizzly bears, wolves, salmon, and other species. It would bar new road building, logging, mining, and oil and gas development on those federal lands, while funding a Forest Service 'Wildlands Recovery Corps' to restore damaged areas and recognizing Blackfeet treaty rights in the Badger-Two Medicine area.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who use public lands — hikers, hunters, anglers, and paddlers — would gain permanently protected wild country. Communities downstream of the Rockies would benefit from protected headwaters that supply clean water. The Blackfeet Nation would gain formal recognition of its 1896 treaty rights and guaranteed access for traditional and religious uses, and the bill would create restoration jobs through a new Wildlands Recovery Corps.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public-lands users, tribes, and rural restoration workers

how_it_helps.text: Designates wilderness, wild and scenic rivers, and biological connecting corridors across Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming, permanently protecting habitat for threatened species such as grizzly bears, wolves, caribou, and salmon.

Prohibits new road construction, timber harvesting, mining, oil and gas leasing, and dams on the protected lands, which the bill's findings say would otherwise be developed at public expense and fragment the last intact wild ecosystem south of Canada.

Recognizes that the Blackfeet Nation retains treaty rights in the Badger-Two Medicine area, guarantees Native Americans access to designated areas for traditional cultural and religious purposes, and requires cooperative management agreements with tribes.
Authorizes appropriations for a National Wildland Recovery Corps, a special unit of the Forest Service, to restore damaged wild lands — creating public-works jobs in the region.

analysis.who_pays: The timber, mining, and oil and gas industries would lose access to millions of acres of federal land they currently log, mine, or lease, and rural towns built around logging would bear the adjustment costs. The Treasury would fund the Wildlands Recovery Corps and wilderness management.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies

drawbacks.text: The bill bans timber harvesting, mining, and oil and gas leasing across the designated lands, which would end logging activity and the jobs and county revenue that depend on it in forest towns across the five states.

The scale is unusually large — the wilderness designations alone total roughly 11 million acres plus about 4.5 million acres of corridors — which critics argued was too much land set aside at once for regional economies and local management input.
Designating land as wilderness generally prohibits motorized access, so some hunters, snowmobilers, and off-road users would lose access to areas they currently use.
The bill authorizes new federal spending for the Wildlands Recovery Corps and wilderness management without identifying an offsetting funding source.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded a permanent public good — intact wilderness, clean headwaters, and endangered-species habitat used by millions of Americans — for the curtailment of extractive industries on federal land. The costs fall on a concentrated set of firms and on some rural logging communities, and the scale of the designations drew legitimate regional objections; but the bill's own findings argue the undeveloped lands are worth more to the nation left unlogged than as timber, and much of that timber historically sold below cost. On balance the design favors the public, though a phased approach could have softened the blow to logging towns.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees and its subcommittees held hearings in the spring of 1994, but no committee ever voted to send it to the full House, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Introduced on July 14, 1993 by Rep. Carolyn Maloney with three original cosponsors and referred jointly to the Agriculture, Natural Resources, and Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committees.
Sixty-four members cosponsored the bill: 54 Democrats, 9 Republicans, and 1 Independent.
Subcommittee hearings were held in April 1994, including joint hearings by two subcommittees in May 1994, and the Interior Department and USDA were asked for their views.
No committee reported the bill out, and no floor vote ever occurred; the Congress ended on January 3, 1995 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests kept unrestricted access to the federal roadless lands, and no wilderness protections or restoration program were created. Public-lands users gained nothing from the bill's death except the status quo of continued development on those lands.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 24 additional sponsors in its first two months.

for.name: 64 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it one of the larger cross-party coalitions for a lands bill of that Congress.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 14, 1993 and never reported it out or scheduled a markup; the bill was also divided among three committees, any one of which could have kept it from the floor.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee and its subcommittees
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees, which held hearings in April and May 1994 but never advanced the bill to full committee or the floor.

against.name: Northwest timber and mining interests
against.what_they_did: Opposed wilderness designations of this scale in the Northern Rockies, which would have ended logging and mining on millions of acres of federal land.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Democratic — 54 Democrats to 9 Republicans and 1 Independent — showing the bill's base was its own party, with a small bipartisan fringe.

industries.note: The bill bans timber harvesting on roughly 11 million acres of designated wilderness and most corridor lands, ending logging on federal roadless forests. The industry's interest in keeping those lands open to harvest runs against the public's interest in intact forests and clean headwaters.

The bill withdraws the Badger-Two Medicine area and corridor lands from entry under the mining laws and bans mining on protected lands. Federal land mining profits privatize gains while the environmental costs fall on the public.

The bill prohibits oil and gas leasing and development on the designated wilderness, corridors, study areas, and remaining roadless lands. Companies currently lease or could lease those federal lands at terms that leave development costs — including habitat loss — to the public.

Permanent wilderness and wild and scenic river designations protect the scenery, fisheries, and wild country that drive recreation economies in gateway towns. Wilderness rules would restrict motorized recreation, a narrower loss within an overall gain.
